title: The Legend of Sedna
summary: A girl cast into the sea by her own father becomes the goddess of marine animals, and only the shaman who braids her tangled hair can release the creatures she withholds.
full_text:
In the time before memory, there lived a girl named Sedna on the shore of the great northern sea. She was beautiful — the most beautiful girl her village had ever seen. Her hair was black as the winter ocean, and her eyes held the depth of ice caves. She was kind and clever, and her father loved her above all things.

But Sedna was restless. She dreamed of the sea. Every morning, she walked to the water's edge and stared at the horizon, where the sky met the ice. She wanted to go beyond the shore, beyond the ice floes, to the place where the water had no bottom.

One day, a stranger came to the village. He was tall and handsome, dressed in fine furs. He told Sedna he was a great hunter from a distant island, and he offered her a life of plenty — fat seals, warm pelts, a house that never leaked. Sedna agreed to go with him.

Her father begged her to stay. 'The sea does not give back what it takes,' he said. But Sedna was young and proud. She climbed into the stranger's kayak, and they paddled away.

They traveled for days. The seals disappeared. The fish vanished. The ice grew thin and treacherous. Sedna looked at her new home — a bare rock in the middle of the ocean, with nothing but wind and salt. She looked at her husband, and saw that he was not a man at all. He was a storm petrel — a great sea bird in human form. His hands were talons. His eyes were black and unblinking.

Sedna screamed. She ran to the water's edge and called for her father. Her father, who had followed in his kayak, heard her cries. He paddled to the rock and reached out his hand. Sedna leaped into the kayak.

The storm petrel saw her escape. He beat his wings and called to the sea. The ocean rose — a great wall of black water that surged toward the kayak. Sedna's father looked at the wave, then at his daughter, then at his own hands. He made a choice.

He threw Sedna into the sea.

She hit the water like a stone. The cold was beyond anything she had ever felt — a cold that burned, that paralyzed, that reached into her bones and pulled. She sank. The water closed over her head.

But Sedna did not die. The cold transformed her. Her fingers became seals. Her toes became walruses. Her hair became whales and dolphins and the thousand swimming things of the ocean. Her body became the sea floor, and from it grew all the creatures that the hunters needed to survive.

She became Sedna — the Mother of the Sea, the Keeper of Animals.

Her father, paddling away in his kayak, felt the sea turn against him. The seals vanished. The fish disappeared. His people starved. He knew what he had done.

The village shaman, an old woman named Kaarak, prepared to dive. She cut her hair and braided it into a rope. She dove from the kayak, down through the black water, past the ice, past the darkness, to the very bottom of the sea.

There she found Sedna. Her hair was tangled — matted with sand and shells and the debris of the ocean floor. Kaarak took Sedna's hair in her hands and began to braid. She braided slowly, carefully, singing as she worked. As each braid was completed, Sedna released a seal. Another braid — a walrus. Another — a whale.

Sedna's hair was long, and the braiding took hours. But Kaarak did not stop. She braided until her fingers were numb and her lungs burned. When the last braid was finished, the sea was full of life again.

Kaarak returned to the surface, gasping. The seals were back. The fish swarmed. The hunters could eat.

But the shaman warned the village: Sedna's hair tangles easily. When she is angry — when hunters take too much, when they waste what they are given, when they break the old laws — her hair knots, and the animals disappear. Only the shaman can dive to comb it free.

This is why the people take only what they need. This is why they thank the animals they kill. This is why they leave offerings at the water's edge.

Because Sedna remembers. And she never forgets a debt.
moral: Take only what you need from the sea. The creatures are gifts, and those who waste them will find the gifts withdrawn.
source: Based on Inuit oral traditions from the Canadian Arctic, particularly as recorded by Knud Rasmussen and Diamond Jenness.

title: The Qalupalik
summary: A humanoid sea creature with green skin and long fingernails drags children who wander too close to the ice edge beneath the water.
full_text:
Every Inuit parent knows the warning: do not go near the ice edge. Do not play on the floes. Do not wander where the sea meets the land in the long twilight of winter. Because the Qalupalik is waiting.

She is not a seal. She is not a whale. She is something older — a woman who chose the sea over the land, who gave up her humanity to become something that could never be seen in daylight. She has skin the color of deep water — green-blue, like ice seen from below. Her hair is long and tangled, drifting around her like seaweed. Her fingernails are curved and sharp, like the claws of a crab. And her eyes — her eyes are the pale, dead white of the ice that forms in the cracks between worlds.

She cannot walk on land. The land rejects her. But she can swim beneath the ice, silently, without a sound. She can hear footsteps on the surface — the weight of a child, the lightness of their bones. She can feel the vibrations of laughter, of games, of the small bodies that run and jump on the ice.

When she finds a child alone near the ice edge, she reaches up. Her green hand closes around the child's ankle. She pulls. The ice cracks. The child slides into the black water. The Qalupalik wraps the child in her kelp-like hair and drags them down, down, down to her home beneath the ice.

The child does not drown. The Qalupalik feeds them — strange food, cold food, food that keeps them alive but changes them. The child's skin turns blue. Their eyes grow pale. They forget their parents' names. They forget the warmth of the qamutiik (sled), the smell of seal oil, the sound of their mother's voice.

Years pass. The child grows into a strange creature — neither human nor Qalupalik, but something in between. And then, one day, the Qalupalik brings them to the surface. She carries them to a village, far from their home, and leaves them on the shore.

The villagers find the creature. They do not recognize it. It is blue-skinned, pale-eyed, and it speaks in a language they do not understand. Sometimes it weeps. Sometimes it sings songs that sound like the wind over ice. Sometimes it reaches toward the sea with hands that are almost human.

The shamans know what it is. They know the Qalupalik's bargain: she takes children and returns them, changed, as a warning. 'This is what happens,' the shamans say, 'when you do not listen. When you do not stay away from the ice. When you forget that the sea has teeth.'

The children of the village listen. They stay away from the ice edge. They listen for the sound that the Qalupalik makes — not a voice, not a cry, but a low hum, like the vibration of the ice itself, like the sound the ocean makes when it is hungry.

And sometimes, on winter nights, when the ice groans and cracks, the parents hold their children close and whisper: 'She is swimming beneath us. She is listening. Do not make a sound.'

The Qalupalik swims on. She is always there, beneath the ice, in the black water, waiting for the next child who wanders too close to the edge.

She is patient. She has been patient for centuries. And she will be patient for centuries more.
moral: The sea demands respect. Those who ignore its dangers will be claimed by it.
source: Based on Inuit oral traditions from the Canadian Arctic, particularly from Nunavut and the Northwest Territories.

title: The Aurora Spirits' Dance
summary: The Northern Lights are the spirits of the dead playing ball in the sky — and if you whistle to them, they will send you a gift.
full_text:
Every Inuit child knows the lights. They appear on the darkest winter nights, when the cold is so fierce that the air itself seems to crackle. They ripple across the sky in ribbons of green and blue and violet, sometimes still, sometimes dancing, sometimes flickering like the breath of something alive.

The elders say: the lights are the spirits of the dead. They are playing ball in the sky.

The ball is a walrus skull. It glows with an inner light — the light of the soul. The spirits toss it back and forth, and where it passes, the sky lights up. They dance. They leap. They chase each other across the heavens. And when the game is over, they go home — to the place where the sun goes at night, to the warmth that the living cannot feel.

There was once a girl named Aluĸ who loved the lights more than anything. Every night, she sat outside her igloo and watched them. She knew their patterns — the way the green ribbons curled when the spirits were happy, the way the blue curtains fell when they were sad, the way the violet sparks flew when they were excited.

Her grandmother warned her: 'Do not whistle at the lights. If you whistle, the spirits will hear you. And if they hear you, they will send something down. You may not want what they send.'

Aluĸ did not listen. One night, when the lights were at their most beautiful — a great wave of green that covered the entire sky — she put her fingers to her lips and whistled.

The lights stopped. The sky went dark. For a moment, there was nothing — no stars, no moon, no aurora. Just blackness.

Then something fell from the sky. It was small, no bigger than a snowball. It landed at Aluĸ's feet with a soft thud. She looked down and saw a ball — a walrus skull, glowing faintly with green light.

She picked it up. It was warm — impossibly warm, like holding a living thing. She could feel it pulsing in her hands, like a heartbeat.

Then she heard a voice — not a voice, but a sound that meant words. 'You whistled,' the voice said. 'You asked for a gift. Here it is. But know this: the gift of the spirits is not a gift for the living. It is a memory. Hold it, and you will remember everything — every joy, every sorrow, every moment of your life. You will remember things you have forgotten, and things you never knew. You will remember the names of the dead, and the songs they sang, and the stories they told. And you will remember things that have not happened yet.'

Aluĸ held the ball. The memories flooded in. She remembered being born — the warmth of her mother's body, the first breath of cold air. She remembered learning to walk on ice, her father's hand in hers. She remembered the smell of seal oil, the taste of caribou meat, the sound of her grandmother's voice.

She remembered the dead. She remembered her grandfather, who had died the previous winter. She remembered his laugh, his hands, the way he carved ivory. She remembered his name — a name that no living person spoke.

And she remembered things that had not happened. She remembered growing old. She remembered the children she would have, and the grandchildren. She remembered the day she would die, and the moment her soul would leave her body and join the spirits in the sky.

She wept. Not from sadness — from the weight of remembering. The memories were beautiful, but they were too many. She could not hold them all.

She set the ball down. The memories faded — slowly, like a fire dying. But not all of them. She kept one: the memory of her grandfather's laugh. She kept it in her heart, where it stayed for the rest of her life.

The lights returned. They danced across the sky, brighter than before. Aluĸ watched them, and she knew who was up there. She could hear the laughter. She could feel the warmth.

She never whistled again. But every night, when the lights appeared, she smiled. She knew that the spirits were playing, and that one day, she would join their game.

And when that day came, she would bring her own walrus skull, and she would light up the sky for someone below.

The Inuit say: the lights are not just beautiful. They are a reminder. The dead are not gone. They are dancing, and they are waiting for you to join them.
moral: The dead are not gone. They dance in the sky, waiting for us to join them.
source: Based on Inuit aurora traditions from the Canadian Arctic.
